newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-MEDVEDEV LETS RESULTS SPEAK FOR THEMSELVES.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-MEDVEDEV LETS RESULTS SPEAK FOR THEMSELVES.

text.p: Andrei Medvedev prefers to let his play on the court speak for him these days.
And, until recently, the 22-year-old Ukrainian didn't have much to say.
But Medvedev is once again making some noise at the French Open, strolling into the fourth round of the Grand Slam event on Friday with a straight sets win over French wild card Nicolas Escude.
A semifinalist at the 1993 French Open, Medvedev has seen his results at Roland Garros, along with his world ranking, decline steadily ever since.
One of the circuit's more interesting characters, Medvedev arrived in Paris that year as a confident 19-year-old who could back up his swagger with a world ranking of six.

Although he went on to lose to eventual champion Sergi Bruguera, by the end of the season he had joined Matts Wilander and Boris Becker as the only teenagers to surpass a million dollars in prize money in a single season.
Since those heady days Medvedev's ranking has slipped to its current 20, not helped by an early second round exit at Roland Garros last year and nagging shoulder and back problems.
As the results disappeared so did the glib repartee, as Medvedev found himself continually at odds with the media complaining he was being badly misquoted.

"I've learned my lesson," said a cautious Medvedev in his post-match press conference. "I learned you just can't say whatever you like to say because some people who come to laugh at your jokes go back and write something you never said.
"When I wasn't playing well everything I said was used against me. I don't appreciate it."

Medvedev had little to say about his next opponent Gustavo Kuerten, but with good reason. Few people know much about the Brazilian, who advanced to the round of 16 by beating former-champion Thomas Muster in five sets.

"I would much rather have played Muster because I know his game," said Medvedev, who after a slow start to the season has begun to show flashes of his old form with his victory in Hamburg earlier this month.
"I've only practised with Kuerten, I don't know much about him."
Unlike Medvedev, Kuerten, who had to chose between tennis and soccer when he was 14, was in a talkative mood after his win.
"I think this is the best day of my life," said Kuerten, ranked 66 in the world. "I'm enjoying this too much.
"I had a couple of wins this year against Andre Agassi and Wayne Ferreira but this is a Grand Slam, it's different."
